Avalanche Bulletin


Updated on 2026-02-15 17:00:00 MST, valid until 2026-02-16 17:00:00 MST.
Valid for: Flathead-Lizard.

    
Summary
Storm snow will increase through the day. Coupled with moderate wind, storm slabs will be most reactive in lee terrain. Cautious route-finding, and conservative decision making is key.

Don't let the desire for deep powder pull you into high consequence terrain.Continue to make conservative terrain choices while the storm snow settles and stabilizes.Avoid avalanche terrain during periods of heavy loading from new snow, wind, or rain.Watch for newly formed and reactive wind slabs as you transition into wind-affected terrain.

Problems
Problem 1: Storm slab.Fresh storm slabs will likely be sensitive to human triggers especially at upper elevations where wind is redistributing new snow.Problem 2: Persistent slab.Fresh storm slabs will likely be sensitive to human triggers especially at upper elevations where wind is redistributing new snow. Problem 1: Storm slab.A weak layer of surface hoar/crust/facets exists in the upper snowpack. Triggering this layer is still possible but it's distribution is spotty. The most likely areas are on north facing terrain and was recently reactive in the Flathead.Problem 2: Persistent slab.A weak layer of surface hoar/crust/facets exists in the upper snowpack. Triggering this layer is still possible but it's distribution is spotty. The most likely areas are on north facing terrain and was recently reactive in the Flathead.

Further Detail
Avalanche Summary On Sunday, size 2 storm slab avalanches were artificially triggered in steep alpine terrain On Saturday, Widespread storm slab avalanche activity was observed. Slabs were size 1.5 to 2, triggered naturally and artificially. Going forward, we expect storm snow to remain reactive especially where it is being redistributed into lee terrain by moderate wind from the south.
Snowpack Summary Up to 10 cm of new snow will bring recent storm snow totals to roughly 40 cm. This new snow sits over a variety of surfaces including wind affected snow, surface hoar in sheltered areas and crust on solar aspects and low elevations. Below this, depending on aspect and elevation, the upper snowpack may contain two more layers of crust, facets and/or surface hoar formed in late January and early February. We have uncertainty around the reactivity of these layers. The mid and lower snowpack remain well settled, with no significant concerns at this time.

title: MVP’s Mountain Weather Update
text:
Lakeman’s Lookout
The following snippet is taken from the Mountain Forecast section of FAR’s website. Bear in mind that it will be up to 24 hours old by the time you read it! Many thanks as always to Ron Lakeman for his hard work.



Mountain Weather Report


ISSUED: Sunday February 15, 2025 11:15 MST

SYNOPSIS: A brief gap between disturbances/dry westerly flow aloft will allow for mainly sunny skies today. A minor band of moisture should drift northeastward from a large upper trough centred off the coast of Oregon-California for increasing cloud and then a 60% chance of flurries tonight. A few flurries are likely Monday morning and heavier snow should follow Monday afternoon and Monday night as a surge of moisture spirals northeastward in advance of an upper low pressure digging southward off the coast of BC.

FREEZING LEVEL: Rising to between 1300 & 1500 metres this afternoon. Surface tonight. Rising slightly above surface Monday.

FERNIE ALPINE RESORT FORECAST (1615 metres):

TODAY: Sunny, a few bands of cloud are possible by late afternoon. Windy at times. High -1 or -2.

TONIGHT: Increasing cloud. 60% chance of flurries during the late evening and overnight. Minor accumulation possible. Low -6 or -7.

MONDAY: A few flurries and then snow, heavier by late afternoon. Accumulation from 5 to 10 cm. High near -3.

MONDAY NIGHT: Snow, heavy at times. Moderate to heavy accumulation. Possibly windy at times. Low near -6.

OUTLOOK:

TUESDAY: Periods of snow, moderate accumulation possible. High near -4. 60% chance of flurries Tuesday night. Increasing wind. Low -13 or -14.

WEDNESDAY: Cloudy with sunny breaks and a 60% chance of flurries. Minor to light accumulation possible. Windy. High near -10. Low near -17.

THURSDAY: Cloudy with sunny breaks or sunny periods and slight chance of flurries. Possibly windy at times. High near -10. Low near -18.

CONFIDENCE/DISCUSSION: Good confidence today. Fair to good confidence of the synoptic pattern and poor to fair confidence of the local details tonight onward. Flurries associated with the initial small band of moisture could be confined just south of Fernie tonight. The computer models are still variable with the timing/positioning of the following far more substantial wave of Pacific moisture Monday, Monday night and Tuesday. Some solutions delay the heavier snow until late Monday and Monday evening. All of the guidance suggests a heavy storm total snowfall however exactly how heavy is difficult to predict. A large upper trough of low pressure should gradually push eastward across BC Tuesday through Thursday. Meanwhile a modified Arctic airmass should gradually push west of the Continental Divide beginning late Tuesday or Tuesday night.

 

Ron Lakeman.
